To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the asset's level can be a decreasing, increasing or constant function of the implicit asset growth rate; 2) the exploitation rate can be decreasing or increasing in the implicit growth rates; 3) the number of firms in the market can have a negative impact on the level of the productive asset.

(i) in the long run, an increase of the asset's growth rate can reduce the asset's level, (ii) in the short run, an increase in the asset's growth can increase the industry's exploitation rate, (iii) an increase in the number of exploiting firms can reduce the asset level in the long run.

(i) in the long-run an increase in the asset’s implicit growth rate results in an increase in the level of the productive asset, and a reduction in the number of active firms results in an increase of production; and (ii) in the short-run an increase in asset's implicit growth can result in an initial decrease in the asset’s level, and a reduction of the number of active firm results in an initial increase of exploitation rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the impact of the asset's growth rate on the industry's exploitation rate and the level of the productive asset's stock, and the impact of the industry's size on the industry's production and exploitation rate.
the dynamic implications of the number of firms in an asset oligopoly.
the dynamics of a productive asset oligopolistic industry and the impact of the asset’s implicit growth rate and of the number of firms on industry performance and asset stock.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a reduction of the number of firms sharing the asset can be a source of welfare improvement.
a change in the growth rate of the productive asset has a different impact on the dynamics depending on whether the initial stock of the asset is above or below a certain threshold.
the impact of a reduction in the number of competitors is ambiguous.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the impact of a shock on the productive asset oligopoly depends on the initial stock of the asset.
the dynamics of the productive asset oligopoly is very sensitive to the number of firms and the initial asset stock.
the dynamics in a common property productive assets oligopoly are not trivial.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in a common property productive assets oligopoly, a reduction of the number of firms may be a better option for the industry than a reduction in the asset's implicit rate of growth.
, in the long run, the dynamics of the productive asset oligopoly can be counterintuitive.
the impact of a policy change on the level of the productive asset and on the firms’ exploitation rate depends critically on the initial stock of the asset.
